newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten says China taking over calm Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Patten says China taking over calm Hong Kong.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten said on Thursday Britain was handing over Hong Kong to communist China in sound condition and Beijing need not fear recent democratic reforms.

Outgoing Attorney General James Mathews added his own soothing words that China was inheriting a "very peaceful and moderate community" but tempered them with advice to Beijing not to interfere with freedom of the press.
With 12 days left until what China calls the media event of the century, mini-rows still broke out but there were no signs of a major last minute crisis for the June 30 handover.
Patten, the 28th and last governor of this wealthy colony, displayed his rapier wit and diplomatic skills in a final appearance before the colonial legislature.
While Patten was saying his farewells in the dying days of more than 156 years of British rule, future leader Tung Chee-hwa was swinging into the spirit of the celebrations.
Tung, once a shipping magnate and Beijing's choice to run the passionate capitalist outpost, welcomed a specially painted jumbo jet to mark the approaching era of Chinese rule.
Lion-dancers cavorted around the Cathay Pacific plane and Tung ceremonially dotted their eyes to wish them luck.
Some 4,000 official guests from around the world will attend the midnight ceremony when Prince Charles, heir to the British throne, turns over Hong Kong to Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
Patten stole the show on Thursday with a shining performance before the colonial legislature, which will soon be replaced by a pro-Beijing assembly.
Asked about his biggest regret, Patten wished he could have convinced Beijing that Hong Kong and its people posed no threat.
He would have liked Beijing leaders to appreciate "that there was nothing to worry about in Hong Kong", he said.
Patten provoked the wrath of China by introducing limited democratic reforms in the twilight of colonial rule.
Of those reforms, he said that it "wasn't a question of planting British time bombs around the community but that it was a matter of reflecting the aspirations of the community".
Britain and China set the terms in 1984 for Hong Kong's return but in the final years before the agreed date they have become bogged down in endless disputes.
China has sought to reassure Hong Kong's 6.4 million residents that they have nothing to fear under Beijing's "one country, two systems" policy.
Under the Sino-British agreement, Hong Kong keeps its capitalist system for 50 years but concerns remain that Beijing will slowly close its grasp on the territory.
In Beijing, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said China would not "infringe" on Hong Kong but he hoped nothing would happen in Hong Kong to "infringe" on China's national interests.
Mathews, Hong Kong's attorney general for the past nine years, said in his farewell press conference China had nothing to worry about.
"This (Hong Kong) is a very peaceful and moderate community," he said.
But he advised Beijing not to tamper with press freedom such as the media's right to cover court cases.
"Press freedom is an integral part of the rule of law," Mathews said. "I hope and expect that will continue."
China's concerns are focused on a pro-democracy movement which has kept up an active campaign against Tung's decisions to trim Patten's democratic reforms.

Pro-democracy leaders have pushed their protests in the countdown to the handover and vowed to occupy the colonial legislature during the ceremonies -- a gesture of defiance to the new Tung government.
Hong Kong and China signed an accord on Thursday formally demarcating their border in preparation for the handover.
Although China is reasserting control over Hong Kong, it plans to keep the territory separate from the rest of the country as a highly autonomous capitalist region.
